claims.text: Superconducting behavior in Al–Nb–Ti–Zr–Hf is governed by proximity effects at nanocluster–matrix interfaces.
Nanoscale phase separation locally modifies superconducting pairing interactions and thereby alters Tc and other superconducting parameters.
Annealing Al–Nb–Ti–Zr–Hf at 1100°C produces a homogenized single-phase alloy with minimal nanoscale compositional inhomogeneity.
Annealing Al–Nb–Ti–Zr–Hf at 800°C for 48 hours promotes nanoscale phase-separated clusters.
Atom probe tomography and high-resolution electron microscopy can characterize nanoscale chemical fluctuations relevant to nanocluster formation.
The relevant structural mediator is the presence and distribution of phase-separated nanoclusters within an otherwise disordered matrix.
Proximity effects at nanocluster–matrix interfaces locally modulate superconducting pairing.
Cluster size, distribution, and interfacial area determine whether superconducting coupling is enhanced or suppressed.
Nanoclusters that act as scattering centers suppress superconducting coupling.
The nanocluster-containing sample will have measurably different Tc and critical current density from the homogeneous baseline.
Nanocluster size or distribution will correlate systematically with superconducting response.
Nanocluster formation may shift Tc either upward or downward and may change the superconducting gap.
A homogenized single-phase Al–Nb–Ti–Zr–Hf alloy exhibits superconductivity characteristic of a uniform material.
The proposed interface mechanism dominates below 10 K when annealing produces resolvable nanoscale phase separation.
The proposed mechanism may cease to apply when the inhomogeneity becomes too large or the composition deviates significantly from the stated alloy system.
Separating interface effects from bulk-composition changes requires statistical analysis.
Absence of a statistically significant relationship between cluster metrics and superconducting properties would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure of the nanocluster sample to differ from the homogeneous baseline beyond experimental uncertainty would falsify the hypothesis.
